name: Platelet PGD2 inhibitors
lead: Prostaglandin D2 (PGD2) inhibitors are an experimental hair-loss approach that aims to block a signal that holds hair follicles back, with the goal of reversing miniaturisation and restoring thicker hair on balding scalp. The idea comes from a 2012 study led by Luis Garza and George Cotsarelis at the University of Pennsylvania, which found PGD2 in bald scalp of men with androgenetic alopecia at about three times the level of haired scalp.[4]

In that work PGD2 and its derivative 15-dPGJ2 slowed hair growth in cultured human follicles and in mice, acting through the receptor GPR44 (also called DP2 or CRTH2).[4][1] The authors proposed that blocking this receptor could be a treatment target in men and women.[4]

The oral DP2 antagonist setipiprant was taken into a phase 2A hair-loss trial after the finding; it did not show a statistically significant improvement.[2] Topical and other DP2-targeting compounds, and platelet-derived preparations that people link to prostaglandin pathways, remain a community topic rather than an established treatment.

chain: Blocks PGD2 signalling at the GPR44/DP2 receptor
Follicles are released from PGD2-driven inhibition
Miniaturised follicles could regrow thicker hair
angle.text: People interested in hair regrowth follow PGD2 inhibition as a route that works separately from DHT blockers such as finasteride. The goal is thicker, denser hair on balding scalp.

paras: PGD2 is a lipid signalling molecule made by the enzyme PGD2 synthase. Another prostaglandin, F2-alpha, is known to promote hair growth, and Penn researchers described prostaglandins as acting in opposition on hair.[4] Elevated PGD2 and its synthase in bald scalp follicles may partly explain male-pattern hair loss.[1]

A phase 2A trial of oral setipiprant against placebo (NCT02781311) in men aged 18 to 49 with androgenetic alopecia completed in May 2018 without a statistically significant improvement.[2] Setipiprant itself was developed first for asthma by Actelion; rights for hair loss passed to Kythera and then Allergan.[2] Another DP2 antagonist, fevipiprant, was developed for asthma by Novartis and discontinued in 2019 after phase III trials, and was not studied for hair loss.[3]
In phase II and III data setipiprant showed no severe adverse effects and no pattern different from placebo.[2]

The pathway was reported in Science Translational Medicine in March 2012; Garza and Cotsarelis are co-inventors on a Penn patent describing PGD2 as a target for inhibiting hair loss.[4] Kythera acquired setipiprant for baldness after the paper, and Allergan took over development in 2015.[2]

timeline.event: Penn researchers report elevated PGD2 in bald scalp and inhibition via GPR44.[4]
Allergan acquires Kythera and continues setipiprant for hair loss.[2]
Phase 2A setipiprant trial completes without a statistically significant result.[2]

card.summary: An experimental hair-loss approach that blocks prostaglandin D2 signalling to free miniaturised follicles to regrow.
card.aka: DP2/CRTH2 antagonists, PGD2 pathway blockers, setipiprant
card.note: Investigational; the phase 2A setipiprant trial did not reach significance.

quick.overview:
PGD2 inhibitors target a signalling molecule found at about three times higher levels in bald scalp than haired scalp. Blocking its receptor, GPR44 (DP2), is proposed to let follicles regrow.

The lead drug, setipiprant, reached a phase 2A hair-loss trial; no statistically significant improvement was reported in 2018.
quick.mechanism: PGD2 acts through GPR44/DP2 to slow hair growth in cultured human follicles and mice. A DP2 antagonist blocks that receptor, working apart from the DHT pathway targeted by finasteride.
quick.risks: No hair-loss product is approved. Setipiprant showed no severe adverse effects in phase II and III data and no difference from placebo. Gray-market or homemade versions are unregulated.
